name: Japan Playbooks::Essential Phrases
description: The core phrases for the whole trip: greetings, thanks and apologies, the basic questions, and ordering. Converted from the original Travel Japanese deck, with word breakdowns, pitch and context for Tokyo, Hakone and Kyoto.

phrases.pitch_note: Low こ, then high and level through んにちは. Some speakers let it fall slightly on the final は; either is fine. Four even beats: kon-ni-chi-wa.

words.meaning: topic marker — written は but pronounced "wa". Literally "As for today…" — the rest of the greeting is left unsaid

phrases.context: The daytime greeting, from late morning until dusk. Shopkeepers greet you with いらっしゃいませ (irasshaimase, "welcome") instead, and you don't have to answer that — a nod is enough. Use こんにちは with ryokan staff, other guests in the corridors in Hakone, and anyone you stop to ask something.

phrases.pitch_note: Low お, then high and level all the way to ま, dropping on the final す, which is nearly silent: "gozaimas". The よう is a long o: o-ha-yo-o.

words.meaning: old polite form of はやい (hayai), "early"
very polite "to be". Literally "It is (honorably) early"

phrases.context: The morning greeting, used until around 10 or 11am. At the ryokan the staff will say it when they bring breakfast — say it back. Among friends it shortens to おはよう (ohayō); keep the full form with staff and strangers.

phrases.pitch_note: Same shape as こんにちは: low こ, then high and level. The ん before ば is its own beat: kon-ban-wa.

words.meaning: topic marker — pronounced "wa". "As for this evening…" — the same pattern as こんにちは

phrases.context: The evening greeting, from dusk on — walking into an izakaya for dinner, or back into the ryokan after an evening stroll. It's a greeting only: for "good night" at bedtime it's おやすみなさい (oyasuminasai).

phrases.kana: ありがとうございます
phrases.written: ありがとうございます。
phrases.pitch_note: Low あ, then high through りがとうございま, with the drop right before the final す: "gozaimas". Hold the とう as a long o.

words.meaning: thanks — from ありがたい (arigatai), "precious; hard to come by"
very polite "to be". Literally "(Your kindness) is a rare thing"

phrases.context: Say it to anyone who helps you, and say it often. After a purchase or a meal, staff will use the past tense ありがとうございました (arigatō gozaimashita) — "thank you for what you did" — and you don't have to reply. A small nod goes with it. The casual ありがとう (arigatō) is for friends.

phrases.pitch_note: Low す, high みませ, then a drop on the final ん.

words.meaning: polite negative verb ending. Literally "it isn't settled" — "I'm in your debt"

phrases.context: The single most useful word. "Excuse me" to call a server (say it clearly across the room — that's normal, not rude), "sorry" when you bump someone on a packed Tokyo train, and even "thank you" when someone goes out of their way for you. Staff answer はい (hai).

phrases.pitch_note: Low ご, then high and level through めんなさ, dropping on the final い.

words.meaning: polite command: "please do". Literally "Please grant (me) pardon"

phrases.context: A personal apology — stepping on someone's foot, knocking over a glass, being late. For small bumps and getting attention, すみません is the better choice. Between the two of you, the casual ごめん (gomen) is enough.

phrases.pitch_note: High は, then a drop on い: HA-i.

words.meaning: yes; also "I hear you", "go ahead", "here you are"

phrases.context: Yes — but also "got it" and "here you go". Staff say it constantly: when you call すみません, when they hand you change. A はい with a small nod is a complete answer. You'll also hear a stretched はーい from shop staff and a doubled はいはい in casual talk.

phrases.pitch_note: Soft and even; the two い's together make a long "ii" before the え: ii-e.

words.meaning: no — polite but can sound blunt

phrases.context: Polite but a little stiff — Japanese people tend to avoid a flat "no" and soften it to ちょっと… (chotto, "it's a bit…"). いいえ is also the standard reply to "thank you": いいえ、いいえ means "not at all". To decline something, like a bag or a refill, だいじょうぶです sounds gentler.

phrases.pitch_note: Low お, high through ねがいしま, then a drop; the final す is nearly silent: "onegai-shimas".

words.meaning: a wish; a request — from ねがう (negau), "to wish"
polite "to do". Literally "I (humbly) make a request"

phrases.context: The polite "please" when you're asking for a service or a favor. Tack it on after a noun — おかいけい おねがいします — or say it alone while handing something over, like your passport at check-in or your card at the register. Often said with a small bow.

phrases.kana: えいごを はなせますか
phrases.pitch: えいごを はなせまꜜすか↗
phrases.pitch_note: えいごを is flat — low え, then level. はなせます drops after ま, and the voice lifts on the final か.

words.meaning: direct-object marker — marks what is spoken
can speak — potential form of はなす (hanasu), "to speak", polite
question marker — works like a spoken question mark

phrases.context: Ask before launching into English, especially at small shops and the ryokan. Likely answers: すこし (sukoshi, a little), or a hand wave and ちょっと… (chotto, "not really"). Even when the answer is no, people will try with gestures or fetch a colleague who can. Hotels and the Shinkansen counters will be fine.

phrases.pitch_note: Low わ, then high and level, with the drop on the final ん.
phrases.context: "I don't understand" and also "I don't know". Use it when a reply goes past you, then follow with もういちど おねがいします or ask them to write it down. The positive わかりました (wakarimashita, "got it") is just as useful for confirming directions.

phrases.kana: もういちど おねがいします
phrases.written: もう一度お願いします。
phrases.pitch_note: Even and level through もういちど; おねがいします climbs after お and drops just before the final す: "onegai-shimas".

words.meaning: one time — いち (one) + ど, the counter for occurrences

phrases.context: Ask someone to repeat themselves. Most people will say it again more slowly or switch to pointing. If it's still too fast, ask them to write it — ここに かいてください — or hand over your phone with a translation app open.

phrases.kana: トイレ[といれ]は どこですか
phrases.pitch: トꜜイレは どꜜこですか↗
phrases.pitch_note: トイレ starts high and drops after ト. どこ also starts high and drops; then the voice lifts on the final か.

words.meaning: toilet — a katakana loanword from "toilet"; the small hiragana above shows the reading

phrases.context: Public toilets are everywhere — stations, department stores and every convenience store — and they're free and clean. Signs often say お手洗い (otearai) or 化粧室 (keshōshitsu), but the pictograms are universal. おてあらいは どこですか is the slightly more polite version.

phrases.kana: えきは どこですか
phrases.pitch: えꜜきは どꜜこですか↗
phrases.pitch_note: えき starts high and drops after え; どこ starts high and drops; lift on the final か.
phrases.context: The universal "where is…" skeleton: 〜は どこですか. Swap えき for anything — ホテル (hoteru), バスてい (basutei, bus stop), しんかんせん (shinkansen). People will often walk you partway rather than explain. Big stations have several: in Kyoto, JR, Hankyu, Keihan and the subway are in different places, so name the line if you know it.

phrases.pitch_note: High い, then dropping through くらです, with a lift on the final か.

words.meaning: question marker. The subject is left out, as Japanese often does — just point at the item

phrases.context: Prices are almost always displayed, so you'll mostly use this at markets — Nishiki Market in Kyoto, the Tsukiji outer market in Tokyo — and small shops. The answer is a number plus えん (en, yen). If it flies past, staff will show the figure on the register or a calculator.

phrases.english: This one, please / I'll take this
phrases.pitch_note: これを is flat — low こ, then level. ください rises after く and drops just before the final い.

words.meaning: this (thing near me) — それ (sore) is near the other person, あれ (are) is far from both
"please give (me)" — from くださる (kudasaru), the honorific "to give"

phrases.context: Point and say it: picture menus, food displays, souvenir shelves. Use それ (sore) if it's nearer the staff. To add a count, これを ひとつ ください (hitotsu, one). 〜を ください works with any noun you can point at.

phrases.pitch_note: みずを is flat — low み, then level. ください drops just before the final い.
phrases.context: Tap water is free at restaurants and usually arrives without asking; this is for a refill or when it doesn't. Many places call it おひや (ohiya). Bottled water at a konbini is about a hundred yen — worth grabbing before the walk up Fushimi Inari.

phrases.kana: おかいけい おねがいします
phrases.pitch_note: おかいけい is level — low お, then even. おねがいします climbs after お and drops just before the final す: "onegai-shimas".

words.meaning: polite prefix, common on money and food words

phrases.context: Catch the server's eye and say it, or make a small X with your index fingers — the standard "check, please" gesture. You'll usually be handed a slip to take to the register by the door. No tipping, anywhere; it would be politely refused.

phrases.pitch_note: Low お, then high through いし, dropping on the last い and staying low through です.

words.meaning: delicious — an い-adjective, a complete sentence by itself
politeness marker — adds formality, not meaning

phrases.context: Say it to the chef at a counter, to the staff serving the kaiseki dinner at the ryokan, or to each other — people love hearing it. You'll also hear いただきます (itadakimasu) before a meal and ごちそうさまでした (gochisōsama deshita) after; saying the latter on the way out is a lovely touch.

phrases.english: I'm okay / It's fine / No thank you
phrases.pitch_note: Low だ, high いじょ, then dropping on the long うぶ and staying low through です: dai-JO-o-bu-des.
phrases.context: Three uses in one: "I'm fine" when someone checks on you, "it's fine" when someone apologizes, and a soft "no thank you" — the polite way to turn down a bag at the register or a refill. A small hand wave makes the refusal clear. As a question, だいじょうぶですか, it's "are you okay?"

phrases.pitch_note: The よう is a long o: sa-yo-o-na-ra. Let the pitch fall gently toward the end.

words.meaning: "if it is (so)". Literally "If that is so, (then we part)" — the farewell trails off, like こんにちは

phrases.context: Formal and a little final — more "farewell" than "bye", so you'll rarely need it. Leaving a shop or restaurant, staff say ありがとうございました and a nod or the same back is plenty. For hosts you've gotten to know, like the ryokan staff, おせわに なりました (osewa ni narimashita, "thank you for looking after us") is the warm choice. Casual: じゃあね (jā ne), またね (mata ne).
